title: Money in Campaigns
short: Federal law limits and discloses contributions to candidates (FECA, 1971; BCRA, 2002); Buckley v. Valeo (1976) treated spending as protected speech; Citizens United v. FEC (2010) held the government may not limit independent spending by corporations and unions, which led to super PACs.
trouble: Students think Citizens United allows unlimited donations directly to candidates. Direct contributions to candidates are still limited; the ruling concerned independent spending.

blocks.html: Campaigns cost money: ads, staff, travel. After the Watergate scandal, Congress strengthened the rules. Today's rules come from laws and from Supreme Court cases about the First Amendment, the same freedom of speech you studied.

head: Law or case
Year
What it did
rows: Required disclosure of contributions; the 1974 amendments set limits and created the Federal Election Commission (FEC)
Limits on contributions to candidates are allowed; limits on candidates' own spending and on independent expenditures are not: spending money to communicate is protected speech
Banned national parties' unlimited "soft money" and limited some corporate and union-funded ads before elections
The government may not ban independent election spending by corporations and unions
Groups that may raise and spend unlimited amounts, but only independently: they may not give to or coordinate with candidates

blocks.html: The debate turns on two values. Supporters of limits say large sums can buy influence, or look as if they do, and drown out ordinary voters; the Court has accepted preventing corruption and its appearance as a reason for contribution limits. Opponents say political speech costs money, and limiting spending limits speech; the government should not decide how much speech is too much. Disclosure has drawn wider support: most donations to candidates and parties must be reported, so voters can see who gives. Contribution limits still apply: for 2025 and 2026, an individual may give a federal candidate up to 3,500 dollars per election (primary and general count separately), an amount the FEC adjusts for inflation.

blocks.title: Allowed?
blocks.q: After Citizens United, may a corporation give 1 million dollars directly to a Senate candidate's campaign?
steps: Citizens United concerned independent spending, not contributions to candidates.
Direct corporate contributions to federal candidates remain banned, and individual gifts are capped.

blocks.title: Independent or coordinated?
blocks.q: A super PAC plans its ads together with a candidate's campaign manager. Is that allowed?
steps: Super PACs may spend without limit only if they act independently.
Coordinating with the campaign breaks that rule.
blocks.a: No; super PACs may not coordinate with candidates.

blocks.html: Thinking Citizens United allows unlimited donations directly to candidates. Direct contributions are still limited; the ruling concerned independent spending. Check: is the money given to the candidate, or spent separately?
